formula.title: Cryptographic Hash Function Principle
formula.expression: H = Hash(M)  |  Where H is fixed-size digest, M is variable-length message
formula.explanation: A cryptographic hash function maps arbitrary-length binary data to a fixed-length hexadecimal digest. Ideal hash functions are deterministic, fast to compute, non-reversible (pre-image resistance), collision-resistant (no two messages yield the same digest), and exhibit an avalanche effect where a 1-bit input change alters over 50% of the output bits.

commonMistakes.title: Using Fast Hashes (SHA-256/MD5) for Passwords
commonMistakes.description: Fast cryptographic hash functions can compute billions of guesses per second on consumer GPUs. Passwords must always use slow, memory-hard key derivation functions like Argon2, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with unique salts.

commonMistakes.title: Using SHA-1 or MD5 in New Systems
commonMistakes.description: SHA-1 and MD5 have proven practical collision vulnerabilities (e.g. SHAttered attack). They are obsolete and insecure for digital signatures, certificates, and integrity guarantees.

commonMistakes.title: Ignoring Character Encoding (UTF-8 vs Latin-1)
commonMistakes.description: Hashing depends on raw binary bytes. Hashing multi-byte Unicode characters (accents, emojis) in different encodings produces completely divergent digests.

commonMistakes.title: Relying on Unsalted Hashes
commonMistakes.description: Hashing without cryptographic salting allows attackers to reverse digests instantly using precomputed rainbow tables.

faqs.q: Is SHA-256 safe for storing passwords?
faqs.a: No. SHA-256 is designed to be extremely fast for checksums, allowing modern GPUs to guess over 10 billion hashes per second. For passwords, always use slow, salted, memory-hard algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt.

faqs.q: Why is MD5 not available in this tool?
faqs.a: MD5 has been cryptographically broken since 2004, with trivial collision vulnerabilities demonstrated in under one second. Because MD5 presents critical security risks when used in modern applications, ToolsBuilt does not implement or offer MD5.

faqs.q: Can a cryptographic hash be decrypted or reversed?
faqs.a: No. Hash functions are strictly one-way mathematical operations that compress data, discarding original length and structure. A hash cannot be mathematically reversed; it can only be guessed by brute force.

faqs.q: What is the difference between SHA-256 and SHA-512?
faqs.a: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit (32-byte) digest using 32-bit operations, while SHA-512 produces a 512-bit (64-byte) digest using 64-bit operations. On 64-bit CPU architectures, SHA-512 is frequently faster than SHA-256.

faqs.q: Does ToolsBuilt send my text to a server to compute the hash?
faqs.a: No. All hashes are calculated locally inside your web browser using Web Crypto (crypto.subtle). Your input text and computed hashes are never transmitted across the network.
